executive_assessment.text: The bank distinguishes Ngerikiil/Airai–Koror supply dependence, remote-atoll catchments, rural Babeldaob water-quality constraints and historical Melekeok/Kayangel cultural-site exposure.

Policy and reef-governance capacities include funding/integration constraints and locally designed strategies; planned training, future bleaching claims and proposed works are not delivered or observed outcomes.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2013-09 reports: The assessment placed most coastal homes, tourist lodging and utility lines within 30 metres of Melekeok’s high-water mark, vulnerable to sea rise, waves and typhoons.
Source dated 2013-09 reports: It identified the southern-coast wastewater plant as a low-lying mangrove-edge asset at risk of inundation, damage and sewage release.

Source dated 2013-09 reports: Ngardok Nature Reserve covers one-third of Melekeok and supplies its only drinking water; prolonged drought is identified as its greatest natural-system threat, alongside flood and erosion risks.

Source dated 2013-09 reports: Proposed outputs included resilient wastewater, watershed and water-supply systems plus a state adaptation plan; no project adaptation strategies had yet been implemented.

The 2025 water policy identifies the Ngerikiil catchment in Airai as the primary supply area for Airai and Koror. Its population-coverage figures vary between passages, so the bank retains qualitative dependence rather than a precise current coverage share.
Source dated 2025 reports: The policy says households on remote atolls including Kayangel, Sonsorol and Hatohobei mostly rely on rainwater catchments rather than piped treated water.
Source dated 2021 reports: At Iporu on Tobi, surveyors found erosion had exposed archaeological remains; low-lying Tobi cultural sites (3–4 metres and below) were considered at risk of inundation.

Source dated 2021 reports: The report describes 2012–13 typhoon-driven debris, saltwater inundation affecting Kayangel gardens and homes, and flooding again in April 2021 at the low-lying traditional-village sites.

Source dated 2021 reports: At the Melekeok coast, four stone monoliths had been undercut by erosion and were resting on the beach; the report recommends restoring and reinforcing the site and keeping a drainage culvert clear.

Source dated 2023-11-03 reports: The Rock Islands Southern Lagoon resilience strategy was co-designed over two years by the local management authority and community with NGO and scientific partners, drawing on reef-condition data and community dependence on reef resources.

Source dated 2023-11-03 reports: The strategy account says earlier plans lacked implementation funds and integration; its first phase includes cultural-site preservation, sustainable fisheries, conservation finance and adaptive-management capacity, with a resilience officer placed in Koror State Government.

Source dated 2023-11-03 reports: The local authority adopted a 2021 coastal-fisheries plan applying traditional knowledge to reef-fish and invertebrate recovery and sustainable harvesting for the Koror community.

known_gaps.text: Automated machine-screening is not independent source verification or human approval. 19 of 19 evidence records and 0 of 0 pathways lack claim-level verification in this remediation; review the linked records before relying on them.
No directly inspected source established a Palau-specific climate-to-violent-conflict, violence or insecurity pathway; searches are not evidence that such pathways are absent.
The national communication's detailed Melekeok vulnerability assessment dates to 2013; it should be treated as a site-specific historical assessment, not a current condition check.

The SPREP-hosted cultural-site assessment covers ten selected sites rather than representative community or household vulnerability; its site/event findings do not attribute individual storms to climate change.
The 2025 water policy carries forward some projections from the 2015 climate policy; the separate OCC web page does not provide projection methods or scenarios.
The UNDP 2020 article reports a national drought-affected share and planned training without island-level outage disaggregation or confirmation of training completion.
No full Palau-specific climate→violence or reverse insecurity pathway is supported; water access, remoteness and heritage loss are vulnerabilities without automatically implying FCV.
The official 2025 water policy and detailed older site studies are combined only with their distinct vintages; old Melekeok project status is not current.
